posts.title: How to tie a simple mizuhiki knot
posts.excerpt: The awaji knot holds because it cannot be pulled undone. Here is how to tie a simple one with two cords and ten quiet minutes.
posts.content:
Every couple we work with receives a pair of mizuhiki knots, tied by hand at our studio. Many ask how to make one themselves, for place cards or for the envelopes they hand to their parents. Here is the simplest knot we know.

What you need

  • Two lengths of mizuhiki cord, about 45 cm each
  • A flat table and good light
  • Ten minutes and no hurry

Tying it

Lay the cords side by side. Make a loop on the left, cross the right end over it, and weave it back under and over, as if drawing the number eight on its side. Tighten slowly from both ends until the three loops sit evenly.

A knot that is pulled too tight looks anxious. Leave it a little room to breathe.

Your first one will not be perfect. Ours were not either. Keep it anyway.

posts.title: A lunch for eighteen under the maples
posts.excerpt: Emi and Taro wanted their grandmothers at the head of the table and no speeches. We planned a long autumn lunch in the Moss Garden.
posts.content:
Emi and Taro came to us with two wishes: their grandmothers at the head of the table, and no speeches. Everything else, they said, was up to the season.

One long table

We set a single table for eighteen on the covered veranda, close enough to the maples that leaves fell on the linen during the meal. Nobody moved them.

What we would do again

  • Start the meal at noon, when the light is softest in autumn
  • Seat older guests with their backs to the wind
  • Serve tea at the end, not coffee

posts.title: Choosing a season before choosing a date
posts.excerpt: Most couples start with a date. We suggest starting with a season: the light, the flowers and the weather you would like to share.
posts.content:
Most couples start with a date. We gently suggest starting with a season instead. The light, the flowers and the weather will shape your day far more than the number on the calendar.

Spring

Soft light, cool mornings, a garden waking up. Book early: everyone loves spring.

Autumn

Our favourite. Warm afternoons, maples turning and long, golden lunches.

Winter

Quiet, intimate and often half the price. A timber hall with candles is hard to beat.

posts.title: The Boathouse, and how to plan for summer heat
posts.excerpt: The old boathouse on the Hayama shore is lovely from May to October. Here is how we keep a summer dinner there cool and calm.
posts.content:
The Boathouse sits right on the water, and on a summer evening the open doors let the sea breeze through the whole room. Still, a July wedding needs a little care.

  • Start dinner after five, when the sun is lower
  • Chill the linen napkins with a few drops of water
  • Offer cold barley tea as guests arrive
  • Keep a second pair of shoes for the walk on the sand

Done well, it is one of the loveliest rooms we know.

posts.title: Why your wedding plan should fit on one page
posts.excerpt: If the timeline for your day does not fit on one page, it is too complicated. Here is the one-page plan we share with every supplier.
posts.content:
Every wedding we plan has a timeline that fits on one sheet of paper. Every supplier gets the same sheet. If something does not fit, we ask whether it really needs to happen.

What goes on the page

  • Arrival times for every supplier
  • The ceremony, the meal and the end of the evening
  • Who to call for each part of the day
  • The rain plan, in one line

posts.title: In praise of the weekday wedding
posts.excerpt: A Tuesday in winter: quieter venues, gentler prices and guests who truly wanted to be there.
posts.content:
Weekday weddings used to surprise people. Now about a third of the couples we work with choose one. Venues are calmer, suppliers have more time and prices are often lower.

The guests who come on a Tuesday are the ones who truly wanted to be there. That changes the feeling of the whole day.
